newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair wows press, but doubts remain.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair wows press, but doubts remain.

text.p: Opposition leader Tony Blair basked in praise on Wednesday after an inspiring speech to his party's last pre-election conference in which he vowed to revitalise Britain for the challenges of the 21st century.
Blair fired up his own Labour Party and stirred commentators on both the left and right of politics with a speech deeply personal in content and almost evangelical in presentation.

Even the mass-selling Sun newspaper, which claimed to have won the last general election for the Conservatives in defiance of opinion poll forecasts, was moved to describe it as "the speech of his life", headlining its report "President Blair".
Party faithful applauded Blair's 10 vows for government, which ranged from cutting class sizes in schools to forging a new, constructive relationship with Europe.
Bookmakers immediately cut their odds for a Labour victory in the election, which Prime Minister John Major must call in the next seven months, after a steady stream of bets on Blair.

With polls giving Blair a lead of 20 points plus, and the government reeling from press revelations about sleaze in the Conservative Party, Blair's path to victory has never seemed But aides, remembering a triumphalist eve-of-poll rally in 1992 before Labour's unexpected loss, warned party supporters against celebrating too soon. Blair himself repeatedly stressed in his speech that victory had to be earned.

"The heartfelt enthusiasm of the party delegates for the speech belied the central message for the electorate -- that Mr Blair by no means believes that the next election is in the bag," wrote the Independent's Tony Bevins.
Barring unforeseen disasters in the remaining days of the week-long Labour conference, Blair can look forward with smug detachment to the Conservatives' annual get-together next week.

With a weekend European summit certain to reignite party conflicts over Europe and the sleaze revelations again rocking the government back on its heels, Major will find it tough to fight back in the southern town of Bournemouth.
But key questions remain about how effective Blair can be in translating the media attention into voter support.

Many voters, encouraged by a Conservative advertising blitz, remain unconvinced Blair has reined in his party's left-wingers despite a modernisation drive which has dragged it to the centre after 17 years in the electoral wilderness.
Blair shrugged off charges that he was now too right-wing.

"What has happened is that the Conservative Party has drifted away from any sense of one-nation politics and the Labour Party has now developed a programme for the centre ground," he told a BBC radio interviewer on Wednesday.
He also dismissed claims that left-wing extremists would start making their presence felt if Labour took power.

"The Labour Party is a changed party. The overwhelming majority of candidates support the modernisation of the Labour Party... Those old tax-and-spend days of the Labour Party are done," he said, pledging "sound finance and good housekeeping".
But key questions remain about how he will fulfil his vows to cut unemployment, boost education spending and tackle the welfare budget while keeping both left and right on board.
A Sun editorial highlighted his fragile honeymoon with the right. "His covenant with Britain, his vision...were an echo of the raw appeal that swept Margaret Thatcher to power.

"Blair offered the biggest changes Britain will have seen for almost two decades... Mark our words, if Labour win the election, the Sun will be reminding Tony Blair of his promises every single day," the newspaper said.
